summary:
This run covered 11 evals (60 iterations) on a MediaConnect operations/observability chat agent. Two of the evals (negative-sibling-boundary, negative-unrelated) were "should not trigger" tests — both variants correctly did not trigger behavior and were otherwise skipped from scoring, so they don't factor into the comparison.

Across the remaining 9 evals, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output in nearly all cases (typically 3/3, with one eval at 2/3), while without_skill met expected output far less often — 0/3 in six of the nine evals, and only partial success (1/3, 2/3, or 1/3) in the others. Only one eval (mcx-zixi-bitrate-exception) showed both variants fully passing expected output (3/3 each) and all assertions passing for both ("always_passes" patterns) — this eval does not discriminate between the variants, and notably here a separate LLM quality-comparison judged without_skill's output as favored on accuracy/actionability/completeness (medium confidence), the one case where without_skill scored better on quality.

At the assertion level, most individual assertions show a clear "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" or "flaky" pattern (without_skill inconsistently passing across its 3 repeats), rather than both failing or both passing — meaning these assertions are doing real discriminating work, but the discrimination consistently favors with_skill's correctness on these particular tasks. In the one eval with quality comparisons favoring with_skill (mcx-critical-loss-metric, mcx-pcr-threshold), with_skill was favored 6/7 and 3/3 times respectively at medium confidence; most other evals had quality-comparison pairs skipped (0 pairs evaluated), so quality judgments are only available for a minority of evals and should be weighted lightly.

Runtime and cost consistently favor with_skill: it ran faster (2–7s vs. without_skill's 6–57s) and cheaper ($0.02–$0.06 vs. $0.05–$0.48) in every eval where both ran. This is a clear, consistent pattern rather than a marginal difference, though it's a separate dimension from correctness and quality.

Output consistency (repeat-run stability) also favors with_skill: it was rated "consistent" (score 3.0) in most evals, with one "mostly_consistent" instance. without_skill ranged from "consistent" (on the zixi eval) to "mostly_consistent" to "inconsistent" (score ~1.33) in several evals, and was null/unrated in two evals where no consistency judgment could be made. This suggests without_skill's outputs vary more run-to-run on several of these tasks, which also helps explain some of its flaky assertion pass rates.

Overall, across expected-output pass rates, assertion-level results, runtime, cost, and consistency, with_skill shows notably stronger and more stable performance on most of these MediaConnect diagnostic/troubleshooting tasks, while without_skill shows weaker and more variable results on the same tasks, except for the one eval (zixi-bitrate-exception) where both met expectations and a quality judgment (medium confidence, limited sample) favored without_skill's response. Confidence in expected-output assessments is uniformly high, but quality-comparison data is sparse (pairs skipped in 6 of 9 evals) and should be treated as a lower-confidence, partial signal rather than a comprehensive quality verdict.

mcx-log-surfaces.summary:
This single chat-task eval focused on whether the agent correctly described MediaConnect's diagnostic surfaces (noting it lacks native CloudWatch Logs, and pointing to CloudWatch metrics, describe-flow Messages.Errors[], and EventBridge events).

Trigger/expected output: The behavior under test fired in 2 of 3 runs overall. On expected output, with_skill met it in 2/3 runs (67%) with high-confidence judgments, while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%), also with high-confidence judgments. This is a clear, high-confidence gap in this one eval, though it's based on only 3 runs, so the sample is small.

Assertions: Both of the two assertions tracked (an LLM-judged check on the specific content, and a regex check for "Messages.Errors") followed the same pattern — with_skill passed 2/3 times and without_skill passed 0/3 times on each. Both assertions are marked "flaky" for with_skill (passing sometimes, failing other times across repeated runs), and both assertions failed consistently for without_skill. No assertion passed for both variants or failed for both, so each assertion does discriminate between the variants in this data, but with_skill's own pass rate is inconsistent run-to-run rather than reliably positive.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality comparison could be made — all 3 pairs were skipped, so there's no data on relative output quality beyond the pass/fail assertions.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was notably faster (2s avg vs 8s avg) and cheaper ($0.02 vs $0.07) than without_skill. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~4%), with no compaction for either.

Output consistency: without_skill's outputs were rated "mostly_consistent" across runs (score 2.0, high confidence) based on 3 dimension assessments. with_skill has no consistency rating available (null), so we cannot compare consistency directly — this is missing data rather than a negative signal for with_skill.

Overall picture: In this eval, with_skill met the expected content and assertions more often (though inconsistently, flagged as flaky) and was faster/cheaper, while without_skill consistently failed to meet the expected output and assertions despite being rated internally consistent in its (incorrect) responses, and ran slower and cost more. No quality-comparison or with_skill consistency data exists to weigh against these findings, and the sample size (3 runs) is small, so these results should be read as a limited, single-eval signal rather than a robust conclusion.

mcx-critical-loss-metric.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested both variants on correctly identifying NotRecoveredPackets as the critical MediaConnect metric and explaining that recovered packets indicate error-correction working as intended (not an error). The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so there's full data to evaluate.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in 2/3 (67%). Both measurements carry high confidence, so this gap is a reasonably solid finding rather than a noisy one.

Assertions: there are only two underlying assertions (each checked across 3 runs, for 6 total checks). Both assertions showed the same pattern — with_skill passed all runs (3/3) while without_skill passed 2/3 — and both are flagged as "flaky," meaning results varied run-to-run rather than failing consistently. This is useful because it shows the gap isn't due to one variant failing a check the other trivially passes across the board; rather, without_skill's performance on these specific assertions is intermittent.

Quality comparison: only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated head-to-head (1 was skipped). Among those 2 evaluated pairs, with_skill was favored on every criterion measured (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with no instances of without_skill being favored; one pair was rated comparable overall. Confidence in this comparison is medium, and the sample size is small (2 pairs), so this should be read as a directional signal rather than a definitive measure.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran much faster (~7s avg) and cheaper (~$0.06 avg) than without_skill (~37s avg, ~$0.31 avg) — roughly a 30-second and 5x cost difference. Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the pairs evaluated for that comparison. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.8% vs 4.2%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: with_skill's outputs were rated fully "consistent" across all three measured dimensions (score 3.0, high confidence), whereas without_skill was rated "inconsistent" overall (score 1.33, high confidence), with one dimension mostly consistent and two inconsistent.

Taken together, this eval shows a consistent pattern across multiple independent dimensions — expected-output match rate, assertion pass rate, quality ratings, runtime/cost, and run-to-run consistency — all pointing the same direction favoring with_skill, with high or medium confidence in most of these measurements. The quality comparison in particular is based on a small sample (2 pairs), and the assertion-level results are explicitly flagged as flaky for without_skill, indicating its underlying behavior on this task varies across runs rather than failing outright.

On the expected-output check, the two variants diverged sharply: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Both measurements carry high confidence, so this is not a weak or borderline signal. The single underlying assertion — that the response correctly attributes P1 errors to the source encoder upstream of MediaConnect rather than the network — passed consistently for with_skill and failed consistently for without_skill, which drives the overall assertion pass-rate gap (100% vs 0%). Since there is only one assertion in this eval, the expected-output and assertion results are essentially the same finding restated, not two independent confirmations.

On efficiency metrics, with_skill was notably faster (~4s vs ~22s average runtime) and cheaper (~$0.04 vs ~$0.19 average cost). Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.8% vs 4.0%), with no compaction needed in either case.

Quality comparison data is not informative here: all 3 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated, so no direct quality judgment can be drawn from that dimension.

Output consistency (stability across repeated runs) was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants overall, with high confidence. Variant_b scored slightly higher on the consistency scale (2.67, with 2 fully consistent and 1 mostly-consistent dimension) compared to without_skill (2.0, with 1 consistent, 1 mostly-consistent, and 1 inconsistent dimension), suggesting without_skill's outputs varied a bit more run-to-run.

Overall, the clearest and highest-confidence finding is the correctness gap on the one substantive assertion: with_skill reliably produced the expected diagnostic conclusion while without_skill did not, in any of the three runs. Variant_b also ran faster, cost less, and showed marginally more run-to-run consistency. There is no dimension favoring without_skill in this result set, though the quality-comparison dimension was entirely skipped and cannot be weighed either way.

Both variants performed equivalently on the core correctness measures: the trigger behavior fired in all 3 runs, both variants met the expected output in 3/3 cases with high-confidence judgments, and both passed all 6 assertions (100%) — including a specific LLM-graded assertion about explaining null-packet substitution and bitrate behavior, and a simple regex check for the word "null." Overall, this is a tradeoff pattern rather than a clear-cut difference: without_skill tended to produce somewhat higher-rated quality responses (per a medium-confidence comparison) but took about 4x longer and cost about 4x more per run than with_skill, while both matched on correctness (expected output, assertions) and consistency.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, high confidence). This is a large, high-confidence gap.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 9 assertion checks (9/9, 100%). without_skill passed only 1 of 9 (11%). Breaking this down by the three underlying assertions: (1) "recommends placing ingest flow closest to source" — with_skill passed 3/3, without_skill passed 1/3 (flagged as a flaky pattern for without_skill, meaning its behavior varied across repeated runs rather than failing uniformly); (2) "names entitlement or Router route rather than long SRT pull" (LLM-judged) — with_skill 3/3, without_skill 0/3; (3) the same idea checked via regex ("mentions entitlement or Router") — with_skill 3/3, without_skill 0/3. The two assertions where without_skill failed uniformly (0/3) point to a consistent gap on the core technical recommendation, not just noise; the one flaky assertion suggests at least partial, inconsistent capability for the source-placement point specifically.

Metrics: with_skill ran much faster (avg 3s vs 25s) and cheaper (avg $0.03 vs $0.21) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~4-5%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall picture: On this eval, with_skill consistently met the expected output and all assertions while also running faster and cheaper, and showed stable behavior across repeated runs. without_skill did not meet the expected output in any run, failed most assertions (passing uniformly on none of the two entitlement/Router checks and only partially on the source-placement check), ran notably longer and more expensively, and showed inconsistent behavior across runs.
